speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think most hon. members of the house will have heard with sorrow of the passing of our colleague the late member for Saskatoon, Harry Jones. This is one of those occasions, Mr. Speaker, when the house is united, but unhappily united in sadness and in sympathy. Harry Jones has lost the fight for his life which he had been waging for so many long months with great courage. I know I express the feelings of every member of the house, Mr. Speaker, when I pay a sincere tribute to the spirit which he has shown and express our gratitude for the service he has given to his country.
His career in terms of years has been relatively short, but it has been honourable and distinguished both in the contribution he made to public life in his own community and in his membership of this house since 1957, where he has been a highly respected member of the house and an esteemed member of his party.
On the occasion of his passing, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the government I should like to extend our heartfelt sympathy to his bereaved wife and his young family, and to his party comrades in this house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel a distinct sense of deep personal sorrow in the passing of one who has been my friend from his earliest collegiate days. I appreciate very much the words spoken by the right hon. Prime Minister. As he said, Harry Jones was vouchsafed only a few years in this house, seven years in all, but he has left his own memorial in the many activities in which he participated. In the House of Commons he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs, where he had every opportunity as a veteran to show his devotion to the veterans; he was with the NATO parliamentary association in Paris. On two" occasions he represented Canada with distinction as chairman of the delegation to the Atlantic congress, and in his knowledge of international affairs he showed that training which followed his occupancy of such positions as president of the United Nations association of Saskatoon.
As far as this parliament is concerned, illness struck him immediately after the election; he came here on one occasion and spent two weeks or so in the house. With sublime courage and unexampled fortitude he faced death for many months without a murmur and without fear.
The Prime Minister has mentioned his courage. I talked with him, and never once did he lose that sense of humour and the desire to return to the house and take his part, although he knew that the possibility of his doing so was remote. It was only last Monday when, from what he called the serenity of an oxygen tent, he communicated with the Minister of National Defence and with me, with a view to securing action on behalf of the retention of the reserve forces in his city.
On occasions like this, as the Prime Minister said, there are no cleavages or divisions in the House of Commons. Of Harry Jones it could be said that in war and in peace he lived to serve others. Young in years, his service to his country was impressive. I mentioned his sense of humour. To me Harry Jones was the embodiment of the Happy Warrior. He served selflessly and well; indomitable, fearless, and faithful unto death. To have known Harry Jones was to be a better man.
The Prime Minister extended a message of sympathy to his widow and to the children. His widow has shown a noble devotion to him in these long months of his illness and has been a continuing source of strength to him, and I join with the Prime Minister in extending to her, to the four children and to his mother the sympathy of this house in bountiful measure.

Mr. Speaker, death is always an occasion for sadness, but when somebody is cut off in the flower of his manhood it is an unmitigated tragedy. This was especially true of Harry J ones, who had a real contribution to make to his community and to Canada.
I had the privilege of knowing Harry Jones and his parents for many years. In his passing I feel a sense of deep personal loss. During his years as member of parliament for Saskatoon he impressed everyone with his friendliness and his willingness to be helpful. He served his country well both in peace and in war. We all watched with admiration his courage and cheerfulness as he fought a losing

The Late Harry Jones battle against a fatal illness. The members of the New Democratic party join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in paying tribute to the memory of Harry Jones. We extend to his wife and the members of his family our deepest sympathy in their time of bereavement.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of our party I join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in their expression of sorrow at the passing of a fellow member of the house. At times like this we pause to reflect on the true meaning of life, and we realize that the words which have been spoken by those who knew him best show the type of man that Harry Jones was. We extend to his widow and to his children our deepest sympathy. Likewise, the same feeling of sympathy and understanding is extended to the leader and other members of his party. Death carries its message not to the dead but to the living, and we trust that there may be a source of encouragement and strength for each one of us as we go about our responsibilities even though this experience is a sad one.

Mr. Speaker, we readily add our deepest sympathy to the messages of condolence extended by the right hon. Prime Minister and the leaders of the various parties in this house to the family stricken by this untimely departure.
Still quite young, Mr. Jones could have rendered tremendous services to his country but Providence had decided otherwise. Though in sorrow, we must accept that verdict.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to extend, on behalf of the Ra'lliement Creditistes, our heartfelt sympathy, not only to his family and to his widow, but also to the members of the political party he belonged to.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. M. Benidickson (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the virtues of our colleagues in this grand club of friendship are sometimes better appreciated after than during our hours on earth. I should like to pay my tribute to the late Harry Jones, the member for Saskatoon. Western Canada extends from the lakehead at least to the mountains, and in order that those of my colleagues whose roots are in that region may have the opportunity to pay tribute to Harry Jones I have been asked to say on behalf of the Prime Minister that, in association with the Leader of the Opposition, we believe the opportunity can be


provided for those members who can attend his funeral in Saskatoon on Saturday.
Protocol dictates that I, as a western Canadian born person, might be the head of any group making such a trip. I just hope that on this coming Saturday all will be there who possibly can.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roger Teillel (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext: I believe those who have had the honour of serving with and working for the veterans of Canada would want me to join in this expression of sorrow and these words of tribute to our departed member. I do so with sorrow because, while I did not have the opportunity of knowing Harry Jones for a very great length of time, I know something of his work and I have heard a great deal about his sympathy for, and his efforts on behalf of, the veterans of Canada. It is for me, therefore, a duty and an honour to join in this tribute to our departed member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, concerning a statement I made in this house, with regard to arbitrary decisions by employees of the income tax division in Quebec, and following the denial by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland).
Mr. Speaker, I want to illustrate the fact by a typical example, which will establish that the Minister of National Revenue would do well to make an inquiry in this matter.
It all started last June, when a taxpayer was told in writing:
After checking, the deduction claimed for charitable donations was changed from $525 to $350.
The thing goes on and a letter is written to the official in charge of the income tax office asking him to inquire into this matter, and more particularly, to ask the taxpayer himself for information thereon. On December 6, 1963, that official answered that an inquiry had been made in that case, and that the amount was established on the basis of that inquiry.
On December 10, that is, four days later, I wrote to the head of the income tax office, telling him among other things:
_I cannot recognize the value of an Inquiry in
the course of which the person concerned was not even consulted.
On January 9, 1964, he answered me:
If, on the other hand, the taxpayer can establish that the amount of $525 indicated on his charity receipt has really been paid in money to parish activities during the taxation year 1962, I shall be pleased to have the necessary adjustments made.

On February 28, 1964, I wrote to the director of taxation at the Quebec office. I said:
In reply to your letter of January 9, 1964, I must say that the taxpayer has actually proved the amounts he contributed as charitable donations, and this by means of the receipts he has sent you and which were signed by honourable and respectable persons.
In this case, it was the parish priest. And I went on:
Should you have any doubts in this respect, your inquiry will not be complete until you have seen the taxpayer himself.
On March 3, 1964, I received from the director of taxation a letter which reads as follows:
After examining the record and studying the correspondence exchanged with you, we can add nothing whatsoever to the information already supplied and the letter that our lawyer, Mr. Paquin, sent you on January 9 last.
Mr. Speaker, this means, therefore, that inquiries are made without interviewing the taxpayer or the interested party. Moreover, this morning I received from the Quebec district taxation office seven letters worded exactly the same and mentioning that an inquiry had been made, whereas no inquiry had been conducted.
In answer to a letter sent to me on December 27 by the Minister of National Revenue, I wrote to him on February 21:
I must tell you that I cannot consider that an inquiry is complete as long as the taxpayer himself has not been questioned on the receipts he provided.
Mr. Speaker, the last letter I should like to put on the record is that of the taxpayer himself, after all the evidence I gave to show the attitude of the civil servants of the Quebec district tax office. It reads:
-I want justice, and I shall obtain justice at any cost.
-you have no right to eliminate a receipt for charitable donation without any inquiry, because the man who addresses you is fully justified, he can produce at any time a statement under oath-
Mr. Speaker, I call the attention of the house to the fact that in this particular case as in the seven others to which I have referred and about which I received letters which were written exactly in the same terms, no real inquiry has been made since the taxpayer was not consulted and he even indicated to the minister that he was ready to provide a statement under oath.
That is why I say that such inadequate inquiries are followed by arbitrary decisions which tend to make people apathetic towards the present government and I submit that the Minister of National Revenue should have an investigation made in the Quebec district tax office.

Mr. Speaker, the government is not yet in a position to give to the house a definite indication of its intentions. The secretary general of the United Nations, as I mentioned yesterday, has been in consultation with our ambassador, and he has also been in consultation with a number of other countries concerning their possible participation in the Cyprus peace keeping operation in the form of either providing forces or contributing financially. Until these consultations are completed and clarification obtained on a number of points affecting the conditions under which the proposed force would operate, the government will not be in a position to take decisions or bring this matter to parliament for consideration. In the meantime the possibility of a serious deterioration of the situation in Cyprus is being effectively held in check by the large scale British force already on the ground in Cyprus.
With regard to the attitude of the archbishop, the head of the government of Cyprus, I can only say that this question would depend on the countries which would be invited and which would accept the invitation to participate in the force.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister if he is yet in a position to answer my question of February 25 concerning the possibility of early action on the matter of collective bargaining in the civil service.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMITTEE RESPECTING COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
I have an interim report here, and perhaps I could put it on the record rather than table it. It is to this effect. The preparatory committee on collective bargaining was established on July 25, 1963, to study the problems associated with the introduction of collective bargaining and arbitration in the public service, and the need for reforms in the systems of classification and pay applying to civil service and prevailing rate employees. This committee, as my hon. friend knows, has begun its work. It consists of Mr. Heeney as chairman, and members from the senior branches of the civil service, whose names I do not think I need to put on the record.
By the beginning of September, 1963, the preparatory committee had held its first meeting and had acquired a staff of specialists in labour management relations and wage and salary administration. Since that time the committee has held 16 meetings and the first phase of a program of research and investigation has been completed. This has enabled the committee to identify with some precision the many and complex problems referred to it and to develop possible lines of solution. In the course of its work the preparatory committee has sought information and advice from various senior officials in the federal public service and from a number of outside authorities, including officials of provincial governments.
The chairman and members of the staff have had a number of meetings with the principal officers of each of the three service wide organizations of federal public servants in order to obtain their views on some of the major problems under study by the committee. The committee has also received representations from the association of Canadian postal employees, the Canadian Construction

Association and the Canadian Labour Congress. The committee expects to be in a position to report further and more definitively in the course of the next few months.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
I should like to stress the importance of the Columbia river treaty to this country. The Columbia river treaty resolution and the Canada pension plan, in my opinion, are the two most important pieces of legislation to be brought before us this session. Indeed, these two pieces of legislation may be remembered as the most important to be brought before this parliament.
The Columbia river treaty perhaps occupies a special place. This treaty represents a long lasting agreement, one that will run for at least 60 years. Once it has been ratified by the government of this country, it cannot be amended within that period of time. The Canada pension plan can be improved from time to time. This house, therefore, will have to give careful consideration to the passage of this very important resolution.
I should like to deal very briefly with some of the physical magnitudes involved. The southeast corner of British Columbia which is involved in this scheme has an area comparable to the combined area of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. It is extremely mountainous and extremely beautiful. It has many resources, including agriculture resources. I should like to go through them in ascending order of magnitude; agriculture, then forestry which is more important, mining which is more important still, and finally water.
The great water resources of the upper Columbia region in Canada are perhaps the greatest resource in that part of British Columbia, indeed that part of Canada. There are the water power aspects of these great water resources. I think most of us will regard as even more important with the passage of time the consumptive use of water, industrial uses, irrigation and the control of water pollution. These values will increase with the passage of time, whereas the power production aspect will diminish in relative terms.
What are we doing by ratifying the Columbia river treaty? We are taking waters

Columbia River Treaty which now flow unharnessed to the sea in vast quantities in the late spring and summer months and which virtually dry up in the winter months. We will eventually, of our own initiative, want to bring this great river in Canada under regulation. We will want to control this great force of nature in our own interests, and what we are doing under the Columbia river treaty is bringing these waters under control earlier than would otherwise be the case.
Downstream of this great upper Columbia area in Canada is an arid land, that of the inland empire of the great desert regions of *Washington and Oregon; and to the east, just over the Rockies, is the semi-arid area of the prairies. We will want to control these waters in the short term for power production and in the longer term for these other consumptive uses, and we are going to control these waters by the moneys provided in the short term by the United States.
The United States is going to pay for the construction of these vast dams, and we have title to the additional power developed downstream in the United States as a result of these dams. In accordance with the treaty, we have a right to one half of this additional power, and this interim arrangement entered into by the present government involves the sale of this additional power in the United States. Physically this is not an export. The water is now flowing into the United States, and it will flow in a regulated fashion as a result of these treaty storage projects.
The additional power developed down there is to be shared fifty-fifty. We have title to half that power. Physically it is made in the United States; it comes off generators in the United States, and we intend to leave it down there for a period of 30 years. As a result of leaving it down there we shall receive a lump sum settlement immediately which permits us to build these great reservoirs in this country, and we postpone the importation back into Canada of United States produced power or, if you like, foreign produced power. We are not exporting energy. As a result of this arrangement we are setting up a system which will permit us to obtain energy from the United States, and we are merely postponing bringing it back into Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put this into some perspective. This energy which we are leaving in the United States-and which some hon. members opposite would have us bring back right away-in order of magnitude when the dams are completed under the treaty will amount to about 3 per cent of total Canadian production. It will be a relatively small amount in the late sixties, and it

is an amount of energy which will tend to decrease while our own production in Canada will increase.
By the end of this 30 year period the amount of energy which we will have to decide either to bring back to Canada or to leave down there will be the equivalent not of 1 per cent of Canadian total production but .1 per cent, or one one thousandth of the power generated in Canada. Will we, in 30 years time, bring back .1 per cent of the power which we generate ourselves in this country? That is a decision which will face us in 30 years' time. It is a minute fraction of the total power consumption of the Pacific northwest, and the decision as to whether we will bring it back is ours. The dislocation it would cause at the end of 30 years would be infinitesimal.
Again, Mr. Speaker, there is another way of putting this postponed importation into perspective, and it is in relation to our other energy exports. Today we export a large volume of natural gas, a wasting resource, into the United States. Through one pipe line alone out of British Columbia there now flows six times as much energy as we are talking about in respect to the postponed repatriation of downstream benefit power. We export a lot of oil from Canada. In fact, at present we export more oil from Canada in one year than we will export, or rather not import, in the form of this downstream benefit power during the whole 30 year period of the treaty. This is an order of magnitude which is immense in relation to the commitment which we are entering into through the Columbia river treaty.
I was much impressed by a statement made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. As a former premier of the province of Saskatchewan he made many correct and I think laudable decisions, and one of the decisions he made when he was premier of that great province was to permit the export of oil from southern Saskatchewan to the Minneapolis area in the United States. The volume of energy involved in that exportation is large. In amount it is between four and five times as great per year as the downstream benefits which we are talking about postponing bringing back to Canada.

I think, Mr. Speaker, we should still look at the general backdrop of energy available, and there is an increasing amount of energy available to mankind. The cost of winning energy from mineral resources has been declining rapidly in comparison to the cost of producing other things. Obviously when uranium, thorium and even the hydrogen atom itself are becoming potential sources of commercial energy we should be less concerned with the matter of trade, and embargoes in respect to trade, than we have been in the past. In other words we should be quite happy to sell at a proper price, provided that our own people's needs are covered with respect to power in Canada, and certainly with respect to energy which originates in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I have so far talked mostly about power. I would now like to turn to the consumptive uses of water, and I stress that the other consumptive uses of water will be increasingly important relative to the production of energy. This treaty clearly states that we can divert water at any time out of the upper Columbia in Canada to other areas in Canada, such as the prairies, for consumptive purposes. The protocol also deals with this aspect of the treaty, and indeed makes it more clear.
I would like to read into the record again, although it is already in the white paper, the relevant clause. On page 113 of the white paper we read:
Canada and the United States of America are in agreement that article XIII (1) of the treaty provides to each of them a right to divert water for a consumptive use.
This is clear, and I believe unequivocal. I also want to read into the record the definition which appears in the treaty itself in article I, the definition of "consumptive use."

Let us think in terms of the diversion for consumptive purposes of the upper Columbia in southeastern British Columbia into the prairies. I understand that the general elevation of the prairie areas is appreciably higher than the elevation of the mountain trench in which these waters originate. In other words we will have to put an amount of energy into this scheme if we are to get the water on to the prairies for irrigation purposes. This involves the consumption of energy if we want to do that. Even if we dig a tunnel we have to raise the water. We will have to pump the water up many hundreds of feet before dropping it down again.
I think the conclusion of any impartial tribunal looking into this matter would be that this is a consumptive use and not a definition of use for electric power. This can be debated, but I am quite confident in my own mind that the United States may wish to agree, using the same reasoning I have used now. I think this is a reasonable interpretation of our freedom, our ability to divert for consumptive purposes.
I would stress another point and it is this. Hon. members opposite have stressed the fact that we can divert under the boundary waters treaty. They frequently omit to say that we are also liable for damages created downstream in the United States. In the case of this treaty we have a positive affirmation of the right to divert, with no mention of an obligation to compensate downstream United States interests. In other words, it can be argued that we are freer to divert now than we are under the present 1909 boundary waters treaty regime. Hon. members opposite have also dealt rather roughly with me, I think, regarding my being critical of the Columbia river treaty. I have been a critic of the Columbia river treaty, and I have been an outspoken one-I think, to some effect.
The protocol to the Columbia river treaty makes modifications and clarifications to the treaty. These are important modifications and clarifications. I would like to skim briefly

Columbia River Treaty power benefits has been altered from a background period of 20 years to a period of 30 years. The engineers are familiar with this technical jargon. The base period is changed from 1928 to 1948 to 1928 to 1958. However, there is real significance in that; it means that the number of kilowatt hours accepted by the United States as a result of the negotiations over the last few months has been increased by between 14 to 18 per cent. In other words, the admission that these values will exist is now out on the table and we have been able to incorporate it in the over-all settlement.
I should now like to deal very briefly with the other principal criticisms which have been levied at the treaty. The criticisms follow these lines. One is to the effect that we have not through negotiation caused the United States to recognize more downstream benefits; that somewhere hidden behind the scenes are more benefits than have actually been discovered under the present treaty arrangements. The same people who say this are in the same breath saying: "But we should divert immediately, right away". Well, they cannot have it both ways. Either the vested interests of the United States in our managing our downstream water in this way is a major one-and hence the United States has a vested interest in our not diverting this power-or we will not find it difficult to divert.
In the matter of flooding, the treaty projects do not flood as much of Canada as does the projects of the so-called McNaugh-ton plan. They do not flood anything like as much of Canada as does the McNaughton plan. If you take out of the picture both the Mica creek reservoir and the Duncan lake dam, the comparison is of the order of more than two to one. The McNaughton plan flooding in the east Kootenay and in the mountain trench will flood more than twice as much acreage as would be flooded by the high Arrow dam and the tail end of the Libby reservoir, which extends from the United States into Canada. So let us be clear about this: the treaty arrangements do not flood as much of Canada as do the terms of the McNaughton plan.
The critics are also concerned about power rates. They are concerned about the exportation of jobs. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, by getting money substantially interest free from the United States, by creating vast projects soon and providing jobs soon, by reducing the impact on the budget of the B.C. hydro-because these dams are built for nothing-do we not reduce the price of power in British Columbia? We certainly create a great opportunity to reduce the power rates in the province. We have both

advantages-jobs soon and lower power rates in the not too distant future, by the middle 1970's at least. So how can this be an exportation of jobs? I think this is a tremendous device both for creating jobs and for organizing a great water routine on the Columbia at no expense to Canadians.
One of the great problems in exporting power from British Columbia south to Washington and Oregon has been that in Washington and Oregon there are these vast federally-sponsored multi-purpose developments. Money has uniformly been available at 2J per cent interest. The U.S. army corp of engineers has available grants for all the engineering required for these large federal projects. These being the equivalent of our crown corporations, are income tax free and many of these big dams are more than 50 per cent written off against irrigation, flood control, navigation and the like. As a result the lowest power rates in all North America obtain just south of British Columbia, and we will have difficulty exporting into that very low-rate area. But here we have a device which takes advantage of that unique situation where the federal government of the United States has helped the Pacific northwest region of the United States in many ways. In effect, we are taking advantage of the contribution to the U.S. Pacific northwest indirectly because of this treaty, and it is an advantage for British Columbians through the creation of work soon and lower power rates in the future.
Again, the critics are saying that we should use this downstream energy in Canada, and that we should use it immediately. They are saying we should absorb it and that it should take precedence over any other power project built in British Columbia. But what are we doing? If we follow this recommendation we are making Canadian consumers dependent on imports, imports which tend to diminish every year. If any hon. members have looked at any power legislation in the United States they would have found that if any corporation, utility, or the like, intervenes and requests of the President of the United States that an export of power be suspended, it can be suspended by the U.S. federal power commission. So these people are arguing that we should be dependent on energy which conceivably could be cut off at a moment's notice. Therefore, I say that the most exportable power which we have is the downstream benefits in the United States, and that as long as we have a surplus in Canada we should tend to sell those downstream benefits in the United States, and use our own production from these vast projects which we should create on the upper Columbia in Canada for ourselves. This makes
sense.

This is an arrangement which will not, in the fullness of time, tie our hands. We have built into this treaty -and certainly this is the case with the addition of the protocol-a position of flexibility. We can evolve our power system and water routing arrangements. We have in this treaty the best arrangements which I believe we can make at the present time. We have flexibility. We are proceeding. Many people have asked for action and we have taken action. We have had, in the negotiation of the treaty itself under the previous government, the protocol under the present government, and the sale agreement under the present government, the best possible liaison among several levels of government. I certainly would like to think that every member of this house would endorse this treaty after

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time not as an expert in economics, nor as an expert in electrical engineering but as the member for the Kamloops constituency in British Columbia, which is vitally interested in this treaty. I wish to extend my congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) for their very fine presentations and their attitude towards this treaty.
I congratulate them also on the fact that they have given to this house an essential vindication of the treaty which was originally planned by the previous government under the chairmanship of my immediate predecessor, Hon. Davie Fulton. This was the treaty which a year ago was not spoken of particularly highly by the people on the other side of the house today.

speechtext: A real flip-flop.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
I do not wish at this time, and I do not feel myself actually qualified at this time, to enter upon any argument with regard to the so-called improvements that have been brought down by the present administration and that are mentioned in the protocol. I do want to emphasize, however, the fact that this protocol is the result of having to sell the downstream benefits, and it is also the result of the development of Peace river power which was never considered as a possibility when the original treaty was entered into three years ago. There is no question but that all the surplus power to be created in British Columbia, as the result of Peace river power, and now as a result of the benefits of the new scheme on the Columbia, will have to be dealt with in a businesslike manner.
The sale of these downstream benefits is definitely in order. An important percentage of the economic advantage which is to result from these negotiations has, however, as was mentioned by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, been calculated on the basis of a 92-cent dollar. It was just a year ago that this 92-cent dollar was said not to be in the interests of Canada. Indeed, hon. members opposite said it would be brought back to par if they were elected. It has been shown in this protocol that this 8 per cent on the dollar is going to amount to one third of a mill on the electricity rate. This, of course, I do not dispute; I imagine that these figures

Columbia River Treaty are correct. It is interesting, however, to note that probably through some unintentional oversight the 11 per cent tax that has been imposed by the federal government was not included in the estimates. This was mentioned by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstolse (Mr. Fleming) last July in figures he quoted at that time as reported in Hansard of July 30, 1963, on page 2821, and these figures have not been disputed. They show that the 11 per cent tax levied against the construction of these dams would cost the province of British Columbia a minimum of $22 million. I assume from the figures given in the protocol that we will benefit by the 8 per cent dollar to the extent of $20 million. Therefore, British Columbia will be $2 million at least in the red.
If the cost is according to the figures I have just mentioned-and I do not think there is any question about their being correct-we will be able to count the mill rate as being one third less because of this money and we will have to get back to the original amount, probably nearer to two mills.
These are just a few observations. I do not intend to go into details which are completely on the question of economics; I will leave that to persons better qualified to speak on them. Today, the people of Canada, through their representatives in this house, are making a decision which is probably one of the greatest, if not the greatest, that this house has had to reach for many, many years. It is as great as or greater than the decision to construct the St. Lawrence seaway. British Columbians and western Canadians in particular are looking forward to the carrying out of this treaty which, properly negotiated and with equitable terms, can mean great things for the future of the west.
It was three years ago that, after 18 years of negotiation, Canada and the United States signed the original treaty for the development of the Columbia river. This treaty, while not granting everything to either side, was mutually satisfactory to both sides. The representatives of the province of British Columbia signified their approval of the treaty as drawn up. In fact, some of the features of the original plan which had been suggested by General McNaughton were withdrawn from the plan so as to gain the approval of the delegates from British Columbia, and I am given to understand that General McNaughton himself did not disagree that under these circumstances the treaty should be concluded.
The treaty as signed in January, 1961, contained many engineering features which, as I have already said, I am not prepared to discuss. They were, however, agreed upon after 18 years of study by the best engineers in both Canada and the United States. These

professional decisions were accepted as the best possible answer, keeping in mind certain objections of the government of British Columbia, which features were eliminated from the program. As already mentioned by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), they involved the question of a diversion which can probably be put into effect at some later date.
The treaty, as we already know, and it is hardly necessary for me to repeat it, included the return of half of the downstream benefits to Canada. This power was to be returned by the Americans to Oliver, British Columbia, free of charge. It would have cost the Americans several million dollars, I understand, for its transmission but now they will not find this necessary because of the new arrangement.
It would be absolutely superfluous on my part to enter into the details of the disagreement that came about following the signing of the treaty when the premier of British Columbia refused to continue with the agreement as signed and went ahead with the development of Peace river power. I will not go into the controversy which followed this decision.
It is essential, however, to realize that those on the government benches today have changed their attitude considerably with regard to the agreement as originally outlined. I do not wish to go into all the statements accredited to some of those on the other side of the house and which have been mentioned by previous speakers. It would be superfluous for me to repeat them, but I am very happy indeed to see that second thoughts are, as usual, better than first thoughts. This has been very well demonstrated with regard to this treaty. I feel that this, is not the time for recrimination. This is not the time for harping on the past, although there are many statements which could be revived today that would probably haunt the people who made them a year ago. In my opinion this is a time to look forward with constructive ideas a time for us to work together to create a glorious future for western Canada.
Canada has a very great decision to make now. Hydro power is still in demand. British Columbia has a large surplus of hydro power and will have a much larger one. It will have a great potential for further development. It will take 10 years at least to complete the three main dams mentioned in this treaty and by that time, with the present progress in research, it is quite possible that nuclear power will be available at competitive prices and the construction of hydro power projects will no longer be necessary.

What does this treaty mean to Canada? In plain ordinary language it means, unfortunately, the flooding of some valuable land in very pleasant areas of British Columbia. Those who know these areas will agree that they are desirable places in which to live. The treaty means the displacement of the residents of these areas, and I appreciate the reluctance of the people there to make this change. I understand that the project means the flooding of about 30,000 acres of land in British Columbia. It means the displacement of 1,600 people and the disruption of some municipal and industrial installations. It means that there is a necessity for a study of the displacement and rehabilitation of these people. It means providing homes, schools and other essentials that will be necessary for the thousands of people who will be involved in the work of constructing these dams. It means arrangements to clear the land for flooding and the removal of timber and other materials in this area. However, I think we all agree that with adequate compensation the re-establishment and resettlement can be carried out to everyone's satisfaction.
What are the advantages offered to Canada in this agreement? Economically Canada will receive approximately $275 million immediately for the sale of downstream power benefits for 30 years. That has already been detailed by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. Other payments will be made toward the construction of further dams until a total of approximately $420 million will have been paid. To put this in language that will be understood by people in the eastern part of Canada, this amount is about the same as the cost for the development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
Just how much all this adds up to depends a great deal on who is doing the figuring and how much interest is included. However, the payments do provide for the construction of the dams, indemnity payments and all those things that go along with them, and will probably allow for the installation of part of the machinery at least at the Mica dam. What does the Mica dam mean? As we have already been told, it is a great power installation. To bring to the attention of people in eastern Canada what it means, I would point out that the four power plants at Niagara Falls produce approximately 2 million kilowatt hours of power while the power production at Mica dam will be just a little less than 2 million kilowatt hours. So the two are comparable, and with the further development of the other nine dams that are possible on the Columbia system the power production can be doubled.
Columbia River Treaty
But these are only some of the advantages of the treaty. We have as well a great impetus here for recreational and industrial development.
As a result of the construction of these dams a chain of lakes about 200 miles long will be created which can be used for recreational purposes, for summer resort purposes and industrial purposes. The development of these lakes will make timber limits available which are at the moment inaccessible. A great lumber industry, therefore, will be created and in addition the tourist industry will be given a great boost.
Do not let us overlook one other fact, and that is that we are going to give a great impetus to labour by the construction of these dams. It is estimated that perhaps between 1,300 and 1,400 people will be continuously involved and there will likely be double that number on many occasions. The other evening the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) referred to the fact that we should begin now to think about the establishment of a Columbia power authority. I know that this does not come within the jurisdiction of the federal government but is completely the responsibility of the provincial government. The fact remains, however, that in order to co-ordinate all the preparations for this work, the establishment of industries that will follow, the tourist attractions and recreational facilities, some over-all organizations should be established to ensure that we get the greatest benefit possible from this wonderful opportunity. While the federal government might not be directly involved, I feel they have an opportunity now to insist upon the establishment of a Columbia power authority immediately upon the signing of this treaty.
The question of water diversion has been dealt with adequately from an engineering point of view by the previous speaker. In so far as the right of diversion is concerned, this right was contained in the original treaty. I agree, as I am sure everyone in this house does, that water is one of the essential things we have in Canada. Just how we can best use the waters of the Columbia river is something I am not qualified to discuss. I believe there is general agreement with the fact that if water is going to be supplied to areas east of the Rockies, great engineering problems will be involved and the economics of such a plan would have to be worked out by the engineers. We would have to decide whether or not diversion from the Kootenay area is economical or whether the diversion should be from the northern watershed into the southern part of the prairies. These are things I do not feel I should discuss at this time.

Columbia River Treaty
In conclusion, I might say that I am pleased to find the government has accepted a detailed plan of the 1961 agreement, in spite of their previous criticisms. I am confident that those of us who originally wished the return of the downstream benefits in the form of cheap power will agree that the Peace river development has made the return of this power superfluous at the moment. I am pleased, too, that a satisfactory arrangement has been made for the economical disposal of this surplus power. I see for Canada, and particularly for British Columbia, a great future as a result of this scheme, a great expansion in our economy, our labour and our recreational facilities as well as our industrial development. I look forward, as I am sure all hon. members do, to an early conclusion of this treaty in the best interests of British Columbia, of western Canada and of our national economy. I hope that we will facilitate the study of this matter by the external affairs committee and then we will be able to say: Let us get on with the job.

Mr. Speaker, wonders never cease, because in one of the important speeches made by the former member for Kamloops in Prince George he said, in addition to many other critical statements, that the sale of the downstream benefits from the Columbia would be utter folly and would make us the laughing stock of the world. Apparently the present member for that constituency takes a different point of view.
I should like at this time to deal briefly with one or two statements made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis). I must say, Mr. Speaker, that it is very difficult for a sensitive person like me to chastise such a likeable member as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. I can tell you honestly that in my own constituency I am considered the kindest and mildest mannered man who ever cut a political throat. I thought the hon. member spoke somewhat like a person who has just come to the penitent bench. This treaty covers the construction of the Libby dam and high Arrow dam. What did the hon. gentleman say about those dams quite recently? Thank you. The question of the production of information pertinent to the internal operation of a crown company or relating to its dealings with private corporations is not a new one either in this country or in England. Periodically, passions aroused by some passing controversy involving the policies or operations of a crown corporation have led members of this honourable house representing specific economic or regional interests adversely affected by such a policy to seek information essentially of a nature internal to the corporation, as has the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) in this motion. Now we do not know, of course, exactly what the information would be if it were revealed, but obviously the principle has long been established-and I will deal with that in a moment-that the question of public interest must be left to the discretion of the government and to the crown corporation.
We have heard from the hon. member for Lapointe the same old arguments as have been put forward in the house on many occasions in the past when an area has been affected by such a decision. I am not going to deal with what the hon. member said as regards employment and the various other considerations which are off the point of this motion, except to say that had he paid sufficient attention in committee I think he would have found that the present plan adopted by T.C.A. provides not only for substantial Canadian content, but that there is every reason to believe there will be more employment provided in Canada by this arrangement than by the arrangement favoured by the hon. member for Lapointe. I say this, particularly in view of the fact that no firm offer had been made as regards the Caravelle.
Perhaps a brief review of the purpose and nature of crown corporations would be in order. When government first ventured into the hitherto hallowed ground of operating commercial enterprises, it was in the field of utilities and largely in areas of the economy which private enterprise would not or could not pursue. Politicians of the day readily perceived that if such business enterprises were carried on as branches of a department of government, with the limitations and interferences of patronage and the inhibitions of departmental regulations, efficiency would be curtailed. To avoid such an undesirable result the crown company or public corporation was devised to overcome the disadvantages I have mentioned and to grant the independence necessary to operate and, in later days, to compete with other companies.
There were other considerations. One was that the nature of the independence of a

crown corporation would make it more readily possible to attract to its rank business executives-

In many cases employees might have been reluctant to become civil servants or to work for salaries other than those that were competitive with those paid by other companies. This is partly the reason crown companies were set up in these cases. It was early seen that efficiency of operation would be impossible if the day by day transactions and the affairs of a crown company were to be made available through parliament to pressure groups, competitiors, special interests and so on. So parliament, in establishing a crown company, indulges in a self-denying ordinance with regard to its own power, and the interest of the government owned enterprise becomes the public interest to be determined by the government of the day and the crown company on the basis of granting or withholding information.
The question of information being obtainable in parliament was thoroughly examined in this house on April 26, 1920, when Mr. J. H. Sinclair, an opposition member, asked for certain information concerning the internal operation of the Intercolonial Railway. I am not going to read the full excerpts I had intended because of the passage of time, but I will say that the Hon. Mr. Reid, minister of

railways and canals at that time, dealt with the fact that if the price of coal that the Intercolonial Railway was paying in one area became public knowledge then, despite the fact that the type of coal in another area might be of an inferior grade, the pressures on public matters in parliament would probably result in the railway having to pay the full price for coal from another source. I will only read the final remarks of Mr. Reid, as found on page 1655 of Hansard for April 26, 1920:
I want to emphasize the fact that these questions are not in the interest of this corporation, that they are not in the public interest, that they are not in the interest of the Canadian National Railways...I have taken that position: I believe it is right and fair; I believe the people of Canada will not stand to have questions of that kind answered which will have the effect of destroying public ownership in so far as the merchant marine and the Canadian National Railways are concerned. Neither the Canadian Pacific nor any other corporation would give the information that is asked by some members of this house.
Surely this is the test, Mr. Speaker, whether this is the type of information that would be freely given by a private company. Similar situations have risen repeatedly in the house and have been dealt with in a similar manner as recently as in the last two years. However, I am only going to refer to one quotation from Hansard on this subject which is taken from remarks made by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when he was'prime minister of our nation. They are found on page 690 of Hansard for February 19, 1934 and read as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I should like the hon. gentleman to look at this question with some care. It involves the examination of the internal business of the Canadian National Railways. For reasons which this house has asserted and reasserted, it simply means that we would send a letter to the company and ask them to give us this information. As happens in nine out of ten cases of this kind, they would reply that it is not desirable in the public interest or in the conduct of the business of the railway that this question should be answered. We would be in the difficult position of trying to insist that a company functioning as a national railway should be asked to do something which a company functioning as a privately owned railway would not be compelled to do.
I would also refer in passing, Mr. Speaker, to a book entitled "The Public Corporation" published by the Carswell Company Limited and edited by Mr. Freedman, professor of law at the University of Toronto. At page 72 of that book he deals with parliamentary control of public corporations in Canada and he again outlines the fact that it is a question of the public interest as decided by the government of the day and by the crown corporation which determines whether the information should be given to parliament. Indeed, with regard to the province of Saskatchewan, which has had considerable
experience with public corporation, Hon. Allen E. Blakeney, in an article by him found on page 103 of the same book, states the same proposition, that it is a question of the public interest which must be determined by the government itself. I was going to deal with the situation in England but I will not do so because of the time.
I will simply say, Mr. Speaker, that unquestionably the nature of a crown corporation and its responsibility to the government and to parliament is a perplexing one and involves the conflict of interests, as the hon. member for Lapointe has found. On the one hand, there are the demands of independence and the necessity for secrecy of internal matters that I have mentioned, which in the view of some would tend to conflict with the general principle that a government owned agency should be answerable to the government and to parliament in the same manner in which a private corporation is answerable to its shareholders. However, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett had this to say in 1934:
We have not yet been able to devise either in this parliament or elsewhere any institution that takes the place of the annual meeting of shareholders that subjects the operations of the directors to the scrutiny and their conduct to the criticism that is possible at annual meetings of shareholders with the directors elected for the purpose of giving effect to their wishes in connection with their enterprise.
Although there seems to be no full answer to the problem pondered by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, nevertheless the audit of the crown corporation, its annual report to parliament, the examination of its expenditures by the public accounts committee and its ultimate responsibility to the government which can, in the event of complete lack of confidence, replace its directors, together grant a more than adequate safeguard for the public.
Trans-Canada Air Lines was incorporated by parliament in 1937 at a time when there were no private aviation interests available to take on the gigantic task of linking the extremities of our great nation into one integrated air service. Of the crown corporation that was set up to handle this task of developing aviation, Hon. C. D. Howe said on March 25, 1937:
I think we are getting the best features of government ownership without the application of direct government operation.
So I say that we need to remain away from direct government operation, and that the course that is suggested by the hon. member for Lapointe would lead directly to that. In conclusion I ask: Does the hon. member for Lapointe really want to cost the taxpayers of Canada more money in the operation of Trans-Canada Air Lines? Does he really feel

that parliament should run this air line, because this is what his motion would inevitably lead to? Does he feel that parliament should determine who shall be hired and at what hours the planes should fly? I am sure if he does I would disagree with the hon. member, because my connection at Montreal to go on to Halifax would not be at the same hour as the connection he would want to go on to Quebec.
Surely this motion, if granted and used as a precedent in the future, can only lead to the deterioration of this great air line and to the undermining of our whole system of public corporations. So I ask the hon. member to forget his disappointment that the air line did not in this instance decide on a plane that was manufactured in his immediate area, and remember that in other instances Trans-Canada Air Lines has made decisions favourable to his region at the expense of other areas.
In the give and take of our national existence we must all bear our regional disappointments and we must not allow the feelings of the moment to spoil our perspective. On the basis of the precedents in parliament, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the information asked for in this motion should not be produced.

This resolution, Mr. Speaker, presents something of a problem to the members of the opposition. While I am speaking for myself at this particular time, I think hon. members will agree that we should be quite careful about the views we express and the way we vote on this particular motion. At first blush I would think that if this motion were directed at the production of documents and papers having to do with a government department there would be no question at all about our position. I would certainly vote against such a resolution. I think the precedents established in the past are firm in this respect.
However, the motion is framed in this way:
mat an order of the house do issue for a copy of all correspondence, telegrams or documents exchanged between the Minister of Transport or any of the officers of his department and the president or any of the officers or employees of Trans-Canada Air Lines concerning the total or partial construction of a new medium range aircraft for Trans-Canada Air Lines.
This is a crown corporation, a creation of a statute. It is true that the minister does answer in parliament for this particular crown corporation. There are points of similarity between the liaison the minister carries out with the crown corporation and the liaison he carries out with his own department. However, I feel that if we were to reject the motion holus-bolus as it now stands we would be establishing a precedent that might, some time in the future, stand as an impediment if a case were to arise in which documents should be produced.

Motions for Papers
I submit with great deference that cases could arise when there might be correspondence between the minister and a crown corporation which could be susceptible of production and to which no privilege would be attached. I feel a distinction has to be made.
It is true that the minister when dealing with this matter on March 4, as recorded on page 542 of Hansard had this to say:
I would draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that these motions ask for information of internal concern to T.C.A.; therefore they come under the principle that has been accepted by all governments since it was laid down by Mr. Meighen in 1921 with respect to the internal management of crown companies.
Prima facie, I think this might be so, but it does seem to me that there could be correspondence on matters of policy which would not be related to the internal management of the company to which the same blanket protection should not be extended as is extended to correspondence and documents between the minister and his department.
It has just been drawn to my attention by my deskmate that if some minister were to ask the president of the crown corporation to submit himself as a candidate for election at a certain time, this might not necessarily be correspondence which was privileged. This is probably a far fetched way of saying that there could be correspondence, documents or papers, which are not privileged, and so I think there is a distinction to be made.
For this reason I would hesitate to vote against the motion if it is going to be construed-and occasionally history indicates decisions of this house often are reflected in rather unusual situations some time in the future-as being an indication that no correspondence, no documents, no papers at any time between the minister and a crown corporation could ever be produced.

In passing on, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that apparently my previous referral to the letter written by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) has caused considerable comment in Canadian and United States newspapers. In fact, I appeared in a five minute program on the Seattle television stations to explain what this whole thing was about. In order to clear up the matter I want to say that my purpose in bringing this to the attention of the house was to demonstrate the lack of integrity on the part of the Canadian and provincial governments in the admission that false figures were leaked to the Canadian people, and possibly to others, with respect to the estimated costs of the high Arrow dam. I do not know why that was done, but I think it is most unfortunate and will cause a lack of confidence in government statements if it is continued.

Columbia River Treaty At that time I quoted part of the hon. gentleman's letter-the now famous letter- in which he said:
This is a new figure as far as I am concerned. High figures have purposely been "leaked out" by the Canadian and B.C. governments with a view to influencing our negotiations with the United States. Now that the lump sum price settlement has been arrived at, we are in a position to produce more realistic figures-
And so on. What does Mr. Williston say about that? This is most interesting. It created the following comment in the Vancouver Province of February 28:
In Victoria, minister of lands and forests, the Honourable Ray Williston. B.C.'s key man on all Columbia negotiations, emphatically denied that the U.S. was duped into paying too much for power.
I think that statement is correct; you could not dupe them:
He said Herridge's charge is "pretty stupid" and "bad for Canada".
Of course it is stupid if you begin to doubt the integrity of governments, from Mr. Willis-ton's point of view. Then he said:
"No artificially high figures have ever been used either in negotiations or at any other time", Williston said.
There appears to be a complete difference of opinion between the federal and provincial governments. Who is telling the truth; that is what we want to know. Then he said:
Actual costs of the dam and calculations for the sale of downstream benefits were worked out on U.S. computers.
Ah, here the truth is coming out. All these calculations with regard to the Columbia river treaty were made in the United States; they did not do the calculating in Canada. Then he goes on to say:
They knew more about the situation than we did-they have been working on the Columbia for 20 years. You can't leak figures to engineers of the stature of the U.S. team.
Here is the admission by the provincial government that the Americans know more about it than us and that the calculating was done in the United States. No wonder the treaty is in its present terms. There is another important matter. This has brought a reaction from Washington and I have here a most interesting document. This is a statement made in Washington, as reported in the Vancouver Province of February 29. The article says:
Elmer Bennett, former chief U.S. negotiator on the Columbia river treaty, says his delegation was at no time fooled or deceived by Canadian stories or figures dealing with the project.
"We worked from our own figures and from our own engineers", Bennett said Friday night.
Then he went on to say:
As for the Ottawa reports that the Canadian negotiators deliberately leaked high figures on one of the dams, a source close to Bennett said the

American negotiators concluded during early discussions that the Canadians had neither sufficient background nor the engineering experience to provide clearcut figures at the time of the negotiations.
When these people used to tell me these tales about our advisers, I was embarrassed. Now we know from the top negotiator of the United States team-or the former top negotiator-that the Canadians did not have the figures and did not have the experience. This is clear proof that they have taken into camp our well meaning water resources branch. They are a nice bunch of chaps there; they are a likeable lot, but they have been taken into camp. Mr. MacNabb and all the rest of them, and that famous clerk of the privy council, have been taken into camp by the American negotiators. The atmosphere is becoming clearer every day.
