Mr. Speaker, we are going to seek answers in the external affairs committee. In order that the minister's advisers will have the necessary time to obtain information from their counterparts in the United States prior to the committee hearings, I am going to mention some of the questions to which we shall seek answers when the external affairs committee sits. We want to be fair; we want to give them time to get in touch with Washington so they will have the answers. We want to give them time to put the computers to work in the United States so they can give us the facts.
Let me say, first of all, that the treaty is proof of the lack of planning on the part of the governments of Canada and British Columbia, regardless of all the talk about planning. Let me give a few illustrations. The government of British Columbia promoted the building of a $75 million pulp mill two or three miles below the high Arrow dam. What have they done? They have committed the people of British Columbia to millions of dollars of extra expense-$12 million, at the present time-to instal equipment to take a million board feet of logs per day through this dam. They have committed the people of British Columbia in perpetuity, and fairly so, to pay for the cost of moving these logs through this dam. What a lack of planning. The federal government only last year contributed, through the winter works program, to the rebuilding of an irrigation system in my district. This is as a result of contributions from the federal and the provincial governments. But this system will be flooded out if the high Arrow dam is built. Have you ever seen such evidence of lack of planning, Mr. Speaker? They build new facilities

in the district without any planning, without foreseeing the future, and so on.
Among other things, Mr. Speaker, we want explanations with regard to the protocols and a good many other things. I shall mention a few. We want to know all about the terms of sale, the schedule of downstream benefits to the United States and the schedule of downstream benefits to Canada on which the 30 year sale is based. With reference to protocol 9 we want an explanation of why the 30 year period increases, with regard to energy by 14 per cent to 18 per cent, and capacity by 5 per cent to 7 per cent over 20 years. We want the details of the calculation by projects and by years. With regard to protocol 1, flood control, we want the details of the calculations to arrive at $64.4 million, and of the additional four payments for emergency operations during 60 years from ratification.
Protocol 1, paragraph 1: What is the meaning of the word "related"? That is an ambiguous term and we want to hear the meaning. Paragraph 2: What is the definition of the word "adequately" We want to know what U.S. storages are included in the word "all" and what are the respective capacities to be used for flood control?
Then again, we note that in annex A, flood control, refill will be as requested by the U.S. entity. What jurisdiction has Canada retained over the refill of Canadian reservoirs drawn down (a) for flood control and (b) for power? What provision has been made to make a similar cut in the cost of the storage which is assigned in article IV (2) to U.S. operations and for flood control? These are a few of the technical questions to which we want answers, because as they are in the protocols to the treaty at the present time such are ambiguous.
We also want an assurance that the figures as to cost of the dams are reasonably correct, with the knowledge that the high Arrow dams have been increased from $72 million to $129 million at the present time, and its effect on the cost benefit ratio of storage in the Arrow lakes. The cost of construction of various dams in relation to the estimates provided by Mr. Williston's advisers give us serious grounds for doubt.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that over a number of years the very advisers who advised the government of British Columbia with respect to the cost of these dams also advised the government of British Columbia with respect to the building of the Strathcona dam. The original estimate of that dam was $19 million, the final cost was $35 million. For the Whatshan repairs the original estimate was $86,000 and the final cost was $1,873,000. For the Spillimacheen plant the
Columbia River Treaty original estimate was $1,970,000 and the final cost $2,930,000. For the La Dore generating plant the original estimate was $11,987,000 and the final cost was $19,229,000. For the Ash river generating plant the original estimate was $11,010,000 and the final cost $15,050,000. Some of these increases were caused by inflation and the increase in the cost of living; I am not blaming the engineers entirely. But these are factors which will affect the dams to be constructed under this treaty as well, and we want information about these matters. Already the cost of one dam has gone up from $72 million to $129 million, and we want to be assured that these estimates are accurate.
Many people in the district are concerned about the safety of the high Arrow dam. Well known engineers have expressed their doubts about it. For example, they have not been able to find any rock foundation. They will be holding back a wall of water 78 feet high for 145 miles with sand and gravel foundations, to the dam. There have been letters in the press expressing similar doubts. At the hearings at Castlegar one of the engineers admitted that they have not been able to overcome the problem of underseepage. When one reads of what happened in the United States in recent years we want to be assured that the dam is safe. The members of this committee will want some definite proof of the safety of the dam and a good many people living below the dam will want a definite guarantee that it is safe. We want to know what detailed surveys have been made with respect to the relocation of highways, wharves, and other public facilities, their location, type and cost. No surveys have been made to date; I know that because I have talked to the minister's officials. The committee will seek definite information with respect to the flooding of agricultural and forest lands. No detailed survey has been made. Maps have been looked at and the country flown over, certain estimates have been made, and so on.
Now I want to make a reference to some remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). I am sorry he is not here tonight because he is a most well meaning person and is very likeable on television. He referred to the agricultural prospects. I have not the time to read this report I have in my hand, but it is a report made by the Department of Agriculture on June 14, 1960 on the effect of agriculture and the construction of reservoirs on the Columbia and Kootenay rivers between Luxor and Dorr. It refers to the acres of land which are going to be flooded and says:
In comparison to this there are some 300,000 acres of land in the area, above the level of the

Columbia River Treaty
reservoir, which is as potentially arable with irrigation as the 26,000 acres in the reservoir area. If the reservoir water could be provided for irrigation the reservoir, in fact, increases the agricultural potential of the area.
That is a net gain of nearly 300,000 acres of some of the most fertile land in British Columbia, when irrigated. I will have to show this report to the hon. member for Red Deer tomorrow.
We will also seek, Mr. Speaker, some information as to the basis of compensation which is going to be paid to displaced Canadians, should this treaty be ratified. The minister quoted from a statement by Dr. Keenleyside, chairman of the British Columbia hydro, to the effect that it is not a soulless machine and that it will deal generously and sympathetically with each person who has to move his home or business. I can tell you from my own experience that I was once in Ottawa attending the sessions when these power people came along and put in a power line, and slashed a right of way through some of my property, 100 feet wide for quite a distance. Without even asking my permission.
Many of those who are going to be displaced are very concerned with Dr. Keenley-side's approach and at the result of the first expropriation by the British Columbia hydro authority. On February 6, 1961 a delegation from the area to be affected by the high Arrow dam from Revelstoke south went to Victoria to see Dr. Keenleyside. The report of his statement is still vivid in the memory of many Arrow lakes residents. Dr. Keenleyside is reported as telling the delegation "that they should have faith in the people running the country and should accept their decision as being in the best interests of all concerned", as if to say: What a lot of impudent blokes, coming down here protesting they will be flooded out after 50 or 60 years of work.
Now I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, about the generous treatment of the owner of the land of the first expropriation. I am hurrying to get as much of this story over as possible in my limited time. First, there was a total acreage involved of 37.95 acres. Second, there were 10 acres of cleared land, house and buildings. Third, the total assessed value was $3,450. Fourth, the amount paid by B.C. hydro and power authority was $4,750, which represents a compensation rate of assessed value plus one third. Compare this with what Mr. Williston said. In our district taxes on agricultural land are usually assessed at 50 to 60 per cent of its market value. On the basis of Mr. Williston's statement the owners to be flooded on the Arrow lakes, the Columbia river and in the Revelstoke area expect to receive not less than six times

the assessed value, plus 25 per cent for the misery and loss of happiness occasioned by this flooding.
What did Mr. Williston have to say about this? He said that there were three reasons why the cost of the high Arrow dam had gone up. One reason was because land values had tripled in the area which was to be flooded in the last two or three years. So on that basis they are quite right in expecting: six times the assessed value, plus 25 per cent for loss of happiness, and so on. That is what they will expect as a minimum, and that is what we are going to work for. That is what the members of my party and other people are working for in British Columbia.
The members of the committee will want to know the effect that the high Arrow dams will have on fishing in the Arrow lakes and in the Columbia river. I quote from a report made by the British Columbia wildlife service, which report was kept secret for some time but I managed to get a copy. This report says:
It may be somewhat of a surprise to those who hold little regard for even the monetary value of this resource that the fishery biologist estimates that the cost of compensating for the loss of spawning grounds alone would through the operation of a fish hatchery of equal capacity cost $531,466 annually, and that the original capital investment would amount to $1,992,997.
The report also says on page 41, "It is doubtful if this loss can be made up through artificial means", referring of course to the loss of spawning grounds.
To summarize on this very important question of recreation facilities, we quote two sentences from this report relating to the sport fishery. On page 41 it states:
Investigations conducted to date indicate that losses to the Arrow lakes fishery through construction of the high Arrow dam will be substantial.
Then, from page 45, under the heading high Arrow dam, the following:
Preliminary surveys indicate that the combination of spawning grounds loss plus reservoir fluctuation will result in severe damage to the sport fishery.
The rod and gun clubs of British Columbia are concerned about this flooding and its effect on fish and wild life. We will want to know about the rights of Canadians who are employed on these projects. I want to bring this aspect to the attention of this house and in particular, of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour. I have a document in my hand. It is an agreement, drafted but not signed as yet, between the British Columbia hydro authority and an organization known as the Columbia Hydro Contractors Limited. This draft agreement is intended to cover all the workers who will be employed in the erection of the dams, and the

construction of the generating facilities and transmission facilities on the Columbia river, should that development go ahead. This draft agreement is not the result of a consultation with Canadian citizens. It covers years of work that may be undertaken by Canadian workers and was drafted as the result of a meeting between the officials of the British Columbia hydro authority and a Mr. Keenan, an A.F. of L. official in the building trades section in Washington.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
You have no idea what a storm this is creating among some of our Canadian trade unionists in British Columbia. This draft agreement establishes conditions under which Canadian workers will obtian employment on government projects on the Columbia before a man is hired on the job or work is commenced, and we say it is time Canadians were consulted, by public authorities.
During the hearings held by Mr. Paget, water controller, Dr. Keenleyside, under oath, told the people of the Arrow lakes that these projects would supply employment for some 5,000 to 10,000 persons. This has now been reduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin, Essex East) to a maximum of 3,000 with an average of over 1,300. United States citizens and United States contractors are looking forward to participating in the nine year boom. We must remember what happened in connection with the construction of pipe lines across Canada when hundreds of United States citizens entered Canada as landed immigrants, were allowed to obtain employment on the pipe line, and returned to the United States as soon as the projects were completed. We took this up with the minister of immigration. He could do nothing about it, because they were landed immigrants, and this is what is going to happen this time, unless the policy is changed. There are going to be hundreds of United States citizens coming into Canada as landed immigrants and taking employment and then going back to the United States, when the projects are completed.
In addition, there is the device of bringing workers into Canada under the pretext that there is no man here qualified to do the job. I investigated one such case. One company brought a man in as an operator of a particular and unusual piece of equipment. Inside four days he was driving a truck. We were able at that time to get some 25 of these chaps returned to the United States. We want to know if the federal government is going to protect Canadian workers and contractors in this respect. Is the government in British Columbia going to protect Canadian
Columbia River Treaty contractors? I understand that in Saskatchewan years ago Saskatchewan contractors and Canadian contractors got certain preferences when it came to bidding on public projects and we hope the practice to be followed will be along these lines.
Without a doubt the building of the high Arrow dam will create pollution problems. Municipalities, rod and gun clubs and organizations of that type along the Columbia river are concerned with this problem, and they have made recommendations to the government of British Columbia urging that this matter be given serious consideration. This question is causing a great deal of concern in places such as Castlegar and Kinnaird and persons lower down the river. They are concerned about pollution caused by the construction of the dam and the throwing into the water of tremendous quantities of soil and other materials, and by the influx of workers and others.
We are very concerned about the loss of fish and wildlife, and the proper clearing of the basin. Rod and gun clubs of British Columbia are very anxious that these basins be cleared completely, that all vegetation be removed and stumps be cut down to ground level, otherwise during the drawdown we shall have a most unsightly, unsafe and unsanitary condition. They have not yet been able to get a clear and complete statement from Mr. Williston in British Columbia. However, many are working to this end. I trust everything will be done that can possibly be done to minimize the effect of flooding on the recreational facilities of the district. When I say "recreational facilities", Mr. Speaker, let me tell you that on the Arrow lakes alone 50 miles of beaches will be flooded by the high Arrow dam-50 miles of the most beautiful sandy beaches in Canada.
As I have said before, there is great opposition to this treaty from engineers, from trade unions in British Columbia, and from many other organizations. Trade unions are taking an interest in this question in British Columbia and farmers organizations and other organizations as well as many other people are objecting to the long term sale of the cheapest power in British Columbia to the United States, while the British Columbia consumer uses the more expensive Peace river power. In the second place, they are objecting to this unfair competition from United States industry and consequent loss of employment for Canadians; third, to the gift of water to the United States which will be required for irrigation of Canadian soil, and fourth, to this unnecessary destruction of public and private investments in farm, forest lands and industry. They are also objecting, as I said before, to the destruction

Columbia River Treaty of 50 miles of sandy beaches and damage to recreational facilities. This is one of the greatest inland park areas in Canada, 145 miles of beautiful country providing excellent boating, excellent sport fishing and excellent hunting. They also object to the near destruction of our sport fishing in the Columbia river and to the loss of Canadian control of the Columbia river under article II of the boundary waters treaty.
I see my time has nearly expired. Beyond all our plans and programs, conservation is ultimately of the spirit, an ideal of those people who cherish their past and believe in their future, and are not seeking a quick dollar. Our civilization would be changed by its infidelity to this ideal as surely as by the loss of its democratic institutions, its system of jurisprudence or its arts and culture. In our continued search for the abundant life for all associated with beauty, we must demonstrate both our love for our land, forests and waters, and our sense of responsibility for future generations. If we do not, our haste to promote so-called progress at the expense of future economics, will result in ugliness and unhappiness in Canada for the generations who are to come.

I want to pay tribute to General McNaughton. There is no question that he put up a strong and intelligent fight in

order to force the United States administration, not necessarily their negotiators, to concede that we were entitled to a return on downstream benefits. As far back as 1955 at the suggestion of General McNaughton we introduced a measure known as the International River Improvements Act. The purpose was to stop the construction of a low head dam on the Arrow lakes. The construction of this dam would have jeopardized the general's over-all argument that we had to develop the Columbia on a more orderly basis, and at the same time it gave support to a very effective weapon, the threat of diverting the Columbia into the Fraser river.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised a question about the leaking of figures that would have prejudiced the negotiations. I am sure that if the figures respecting the diversion of the Columbia into the Fraser had been leaked out they would have jeopardized our position in the negotiations to a far greater extent and have favoured the American negotiators.

If the hon. member would just contain himself for a few minutes, he could ask questions later.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has said that this vast amount of storage we are

Columbia River Treaty going to have in Kootenay East, which would be of no real use in so far as power is concerned, is going to be made available to irrigate the uplands. Well, I have travelled over the uplands of Kootenay East and I know them as well as the hon. member. The water will still be there, but at a slightly lower level under the treaty plan, and we will have power at a very reduced rate. The pump perhaps would have to lift the water another 40 feet or 50 feet to irrigate these uplands, but that land will still be there.
In so far as communications are concerned in Kootenay East, I should like to remind the hon. member for Kootenay West that at the moment all the freight from Kootenay West which is destined for the west coast is being hauled back to Kootenay East instead of following that railway line which clings to the crags on its way to the coast. This freight is hauled through the lush valleys of the east Kootenays for 150 miles along a railway line which is absolutely flat. One diesel unit will haul 120 to 150 freight cars over that 150 miles of track. Now, the McNaughton plan would result in the flooding of that 150 miles of railway, so it would be rendered useless or would have to be relocated.
In addition, there would be 50 miles of highway only recently completed which would be either rendered useless or would require the construction of huge floating bridges of the type we have in the Okanagan, and we would require two or three of them. In all probability, this 50 miles of highway which is of trans-Canada standard, would have to be abandoned.
Now, I cannot say that I have travelled up and down the Okanagan lakes by boat or on foot, as I presume the hon. member for Kootenay West has done. However, I did fly over them and if there are 50 miles of beaches on the Arrow lakes I missed that very pleasant sight. We did see a number of deltas. I would remind the hon. member for Kootenay West that on one delta, Arrow park, there is a substantial community. I understand that 60 per cent of the people in Arrow park signed a petition in favour of this treaty and requested us to get on with the job. I am not denying that there may be 50 miles of beautiful beaches, but the part I saw appeared to be rocky, and the rocks seemed to go right down into the water. Any increase in the water level in that area would simply mean that the water would go up higher on the rocks.
I should like to take the hon. member on a trip through the east Kootenays and he would see the fine tourist areas and the wonderful tourist attractions we have in the Wasi lake area. People come from all parts of North America to visit in our constituency.


If the hon. member went up the valley to Columbia lake he would find an area of great tourist attraction. Then, too, there is lake Windermere, an area in which millions of dollars have been spent. This is not a fjord in the rocks such as the Arrow lakes are. The locks surrounding this lake have been completely sold out. We have a highway of trans-Canada standards leading from Calgary to lake Windermere. Since that highway was completed it is almost impossible to estimate the amount of money that has been spent in developing lake Windermere as a summer home for tourists.
The tourist industry in Kootenay East brings in a revenue in the millions of dollars and it could eventually reach the tens of millions. I do not want to belittle the hon. member's lower Arrow lakes, but he must admit that he does not have any direct means of communication with large cities and it is likely to be some years before these communication links would be developed as they are in Kootenay East.
What are some of the benefits to the east and west Kootenays as a result of the decision to build the Libby dam?

speechtext: Carry on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
If the hon. member would like to read in Hansard the speech I made last year, after I have completed this one, then he will see I shall have spoken for 80 minutes on this subject, which is something of a record for me. No more than 17,000 acres of land will be flooded in the east Kootenay district as a result of the Libby dam.
At this point I want to tell the hon. member for Kootenay West that there are also people in the east Kootenay region who will be dislocated and who will have to be rehabilitated. They have been waiting for 20 years for a decision to be made. In that period they have been unable to develop their farms, and from year to year have been waiting for a decision to be made with regard to the Libby project. They now tell me they are very happy a decision has been made, and they will be looking forward to compensation based on a 20 year delay. I am sure this will be forthcoming, and I shall endeavour to see that they are properly and effectively compensated.
Very little rail or road relocation will be required. Certainly those who live on the west side, in the area near the boundary, will be cut off from their natural market, but they too should expect compensation for the loss in value of their land.
The Creston flats are many square miles of land and contain some of the best soil on the North American continent. Due to floods that usually come every 10 years the people there suffer the danger of losing their entire

crops and buildings. The Libby dam will provide flood control for the area, and I am sure will enhance the land values by some 50 per cent, or even higher. The people in Creston have been waiting many years for this development.
Due to the misinformation, or rather lack of information which my hon. friend from Kootenay West and I suffered from last year, we were given the impression that the downstream benefits on the lower Kootenay would be marginal. However the Libby project will now firm up 200,000 kilowatts of energy on the lower Kootenay for the plants presently operated by the West Kootenay Power and Light Company. We were also told that these plants were rather old and antiquated. However, last spring I took the trouble to go over to the west Kootenay and visit them.
All five plants appeared to be operating efficiently. Of course, with my limited knowledge I could only determine this by observation but I did see two men sitting in the control room of the lower plant, operating at least four plants. To me it appeared quite an efficient operation, and as I say the Libby project will firm up 200,000 kilowatts of power which may be provided at a cost of less than two mills.
The entire development of the east and west Kootenays depends on the availability of low cost power. No one should know this tkan the hon. member for Kootenay West The steel industry, the smelters and the fertilizer industry should all expand greatly I do not hesitate to predict that within the next three or four years we shall have a completely integrated steel industry m the Kootenay area, based on low cost power from present installations, and future power available as a result of the construction of the Libby dam. I am also certain there will be vast development in the pulp and paper industry in both regions.
While the Pend Oreille system is not a part of the Columbia treaty as such, it is a part of the Columbia river basin. If hon members would take the trouble to look at the map which appears in the white paper they would see that in the Pend Oreille system one of its tributaries rises in the east Kootenay near Fernie, flows down into Montana, into the Pend Oreille system through Idaho, and back into Canada about 14 miles from its confluence with the Columbia river.
I am bringing this matter to the attention of the house, and in particular of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam-who made what I consider something of an intemperate speech last evening-that one of the benefits we receive from United States storage, 20220-39J
Columbia River Treaty without being required to pay any downstream benefits to the American system, is that it will provide five and a half million acre feet on the Pend Oreille system.

No, there is not that note of contrition one would expect from someone who had made a complete turn-about with regard to his stand on this particular matter. As a matter of fact, I am reminded of the chap who was asked by his spiritual counsellor for a death-bed repentance, and he said, "Well now, taking all things into consideration, I do not think this is a time to be making bad friends of anyone". I think this was the sort of conversion demonstrated by the previous speaker. If I may express it in political terms, perhaps this is one of those occasions when the politician, or, as he used the word, statesman, finds some of his friends are for the measure and some of his friends are against the measure, but as far as he is concerned there is no equivocation at all: he is for his friends. It is going to be difficult, I am sure, to find which way the hon. member is facing with regard to this important issue.
As far as the minister for external affairs is concerned, I thought there was complete contrition two days ago when he introduced this measure in the House of Commons. He has completely accepted the position of the former government, which had the initial privilege and responsibility of negotiating this treaty. I thought it reflected his new role of high statesmanship when he went out of his way to pay that compliment to the former administration. Of course, anyone who faces the facts would inevitably have come to the conclusion that the obstructionist attitude which was taken just a little over a year ago by some of the speakers on the other side was taken for other than factual reasons.
Unfortunately we have not seen any turnabout-face so far as the attitude of the members to my left is concerned. I refer to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and also the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). As has been indicated, some rather harsh statements were made with reference to this treaty. I admit at the outset that it is not a perfect treaty, but I would say it is a good treaty. No treaty devised by any group of men could be the perfect treaty, particularly when you are negotiating in the complex area not only of interprovincial relations but also of international relations. However, I think a fair and honest appraisal will reach the conclusion that it is a good treaty.
I am not speaking tonight by way of any personal apology or vindication. Unfortunately I had no opportunity to take part in the negotiations as such, a fact which I regret very much in that I assumed responsibility for northern affairs after the negotiations were completed. However. I did have access
Columbia River Treaty to the minutes of the meetings taken during negotiations. Unfortunately, it is not possible to place these minutes before the house; even if the federal government gave consent I am sure we would have difficulty getting the concurrence of the provincial government. Only history will reveal the actual nature of the long tedious and complex negotiations which made it possible to come to this rather unique agreement.
I should like to refute some of the notions which have been presented to this house by spokesmen that the Canadian negotiators were not competent to deal with the slick American traders. Some of the men who had the most responsibility, perhaps the most difficult role in the negotiations, were and are connected with the water resources branch of the national resources department. It is true that some of them are quite young. On the other hand, some of them are not so young. I refer to the director of that branch, Tom Patterson. He is still young in spirit, but not as young in years as he once was. I came to appreciate their competence in this field largely because of the responsibility which devolved upon me of answering the numerous queries which were presented on the Columbia treaty, answers which required detailed and complex mathematical computations. I was always impressed by the courtesy and knowledge of these officials who carried the burden and the responsibility of providing the expert data for those on the political level responsible for carrying out the negotiations.
It may be true, as the hon. member for Kootenay West said, that none of these men had paddled down the Kootenay river in a canoe. Their association with the river is not a sentimental one, but I suggest that it does not necessarily mean that they are incompetent to judge the engineering aspects of this project merely because they have not paddled down the Kootenay river. Neither should they be despised because of their youth. I am reminded of the wise retort given by a young man with responsibilities much beyond his years. One who was older complained that he had been in this particular area for 30 years, having acquired his knowledge during that 30 years. The wise answer came back: "Yes, it is quite true; you have had one year's experience 30 times, while I have only had one year's experience five times". So it does not necessarily mean that because you have not been exposed to a given situation for a long period of time you are not competent to judge from a professional standpoint.
The points I want to bring into this discussion, Mr. Speaker, are not directly related to the Columbia river treaty itself, although

Columbia River Treaty they have a very close bearing to it. I want to point out that this Columbia treaty was not negotiated or considered as an isolated project. As a matter oi fact, it was a part of a broad program of development upon which the previous administration embarked. In order successfully to conclude a treaty it was necessary to break through several rather important new areas of activity. As I have already pointed out, this is the first major breakthrough in the field of international co-operation and the development of a resource mutually owned by two neighbouring friendly countries.
Furthermore, this sort of economic development is in tune, I think, with the broader trading and economic patterns which have unfolded in the revolutionary events of the post war world. Canada was a frontier society up until fairly recent times. I am surprised that my friends from Kootenay West and Burnaby-Coquitlam stick to the frontier concept of resource development in Canada. It is true that up until fairly recently it was thought that our resources were to be conserved from the standpoint of preservation rather than exploitation and development. This treaty will provide for an economic development of a renewable resource. Water is a vital renewable resource. It is constantly flowing away to the sea, and if we do not develop and exploit it now it will be lost forever. This confirms the notion I have always had so far as parties with a doctrinaire viewpoint towards economic theories is concerned; they cannot get outside the confines of the dogma of a particular concept.

Another major breakthrough in this resource area-and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has been a leader in this regard-is the idea of the multiple use and wise management of renewable resources, and the conservation by means of greater use in the interests of economic development. The hon. member was one of the great supporters of the resources for tomorrow conference, where these concepts were put so clearly before the people of Canada. As has already been pointed out by other speakers, the Columbia river project is an excellent example of the multiple use of a renewable resource.
The treaty is going to make it possible to use this body of water for the benefit of a


large segment of the population of North America. It is part of the water resource which is becoming increasingly scarce because we have failed to maintain the resource wisely. I have a figure here which was taken from the Christian Science Monitor the other day, so it is up to date, which says 326 million cubic miles of water is available to man in the ocean, in the air, and in the continents. Less than 1 per cent of this huge amount of water is available as fresh water for use by man. It is high time we began to develop and use these water resources for the best economic purposes. Multiple uses have been mentioned-industrial, domestic and recreational.
I agreed with the previous speaker when he referred to the great tourist potential when we wisely use our water resources. The tourist industry has only been recognized in recent years, but in the province of British Columbia it is now a major industry, and there is no reason at all why this development could not become a major factor in the further promotion of the tourist industry.
Growing out of the Columbia river development as an integral part of it, are other major projects in the field of energy. Energy is one of Canada's basic resources. It is basic to the industrial and economic life of this nation, and we have only in recent times recognized that we must develop comprehensive policies, co-ordinated policies, and we must develop rationalized policies with regard to our rich energy resources in Canada.
Only 25 per cent of Canada's hydroelectric potential has been harnessed up to the present time, and yet, with only 25 per cent of our hydro potential harnessed we have been moving rapidly into the area of the thermal production of power, involving the use of coal, gas, and oil, which are all non-renewable resources. Experts tell us that 25 years from now, a quarter of a century from now, these resources will be in short supply because of the rising demand of the human population. There must be planning development of energy resources to ensure their most economical national use, and their most effective contribution to industrial development. The Columbia river project, I submit, is a long step forward in this direction.
The establishment of the national energy board was a major step forward. The establishment of this board in 1958 and the enunciation of the policy of the export of power was a major step forward. I believe it was Right Hon. Mackenzie King who, during the 1920's following the difficulties of world war I, laid down the hard and fast rule that power would never again be exported from Canada. It was only within the past few years that we

got away from that rigid idea, which had long ago become outmoded because of the tremendous changes that had taken place since that time.
The export of power, of course, was logical in view of the fact that we now export gas and oil and our non-renewable resources. As was pointed out yesterday the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) is in favour of the export of oil, and had the responsibility for this when he was the premier of the province of Saskatchewan.
There has to be some progress made in two other areas of power development in Canada if we are going to move forward in the broad approach that was conceived by the former administration. We have to make progress in establishing a national power grid. It is now being demonstrated that the long distance transmission of high voltage power is technically possible. At the present time there is a study under way by technical experts in Canada to look into the technical problems that still stand in the way of the realization of the establishment of an interconnected power grid. Only by a national power grid can we bring into play, while it is still economically feasible, the power resources of the north, for example; or the power that will be generated in areas such as Hamilton falls. This has the most enthusiastic support of the Canadian electrical association because we have already been guilty of wastage of these resources by overdevelopment in various regions of Canada, in order to meet the peak load problem, and also because of our failure to develop the hydro potential before we developed the thermal power potential of this country.
The grid system actually is already under way in Canada, but it must move faster, it must have the enthusiastic support which is now being given to the Columbia river project by the new government. There must be support for these other projects which are part of the comprehensive plan of national development.
It was in 1958 that the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act was passed by this parliament. That act might be regarded as the beginning of the regional plan which will eventually usher in the national power grid that has been under discussion in past months. Just as an example of the sort of savings that are possible by this type of power integration, up to 1962 the expenditures for power under the act in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have amounted to some $10.3 million, but the savings that had accrued from that expenditure up to that point represented a saving of $26 million. This saving will be multiplied many times when the national power grid is in operation.

The maritime system is the only fully integrated power grid in operation up to the present time, and I hope that it is the forerunner of the larger scheme that is so urgently needed in Canada. I can give some statistics as to the degree that the technical difficulties have been met. There are already experimental transmission lines in Ontario and Quebec. For example, in Ontario there is a line of some 450 kilovolts, that is, 450,000 volts which runs all the way from northern Ontario to Toronto. Quebec has a 300,000 volt line from Bersimis to Montreal, some 390 miles, and the Soviets have even made a greater technical breakthrough than we have in Canada. The distances that must be covered by long distance transmission in a national power grid run up to 1,100 and 1,200 miles in the case of the Hamilton power development and the Nelson river development.
I should like to refer briefly to the Nelson river power development which again is a vital part of this whole national concept. We were pleased to hear the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) make the statement in the house yesterday in tabling the report on the first stage of the technical study on the potential of the Nelson river, that the report was entirely positive. He pointed out that it was economically feasible to develop the huge power potential on this northern Manitoba river and, by means of a system of long distance gridding, transport the power to the Toronto market or to the market in the northern part of the United States.
I bring these matters to the attention of the government and the house to emphasize that it is not enough to stop with the Columbia. I agree that this is a major breakthrough and a significant economic development. I agree with the hon. members who have supported the viewpoint of the former administration which they once vehemently criticized in the house. The Liberals have seen the light. They have been converted from obstructionists. They have adopted the vision of the former administration.

The criticism made by General McNaughton in 1963 in the International Journal was, in the opinion of this government, very fundamental and sound. Steps were taken in the protocol to obviate the difficulties which the obscurity of the wording in the treaty had created.
I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members subparagraph 2 of paragraph 7 of the protocol which indicates the extent to which Canada has assured to it control of the flood storage within our own boundaries. The question at issue referred to by the hon. member was as to whether or not by delivering the operating control plans of the United States entity, Canada would be in a position to continue controlling the manner in which the Mica creek reservoir was used, and therefore the manner in which we could maximize power generation in Canada. This objection was specifically met by the protocol. I refer to subparagraph 2 of paragraph 7:
The hydroelectric operating plans, which will be based on step 1 of the studies referred to in paragraph 7 of annex B of the treaty, will provide a reservoir-balance relationship for each month for the whole of the Canadian storage committed rather than a separate relationship for each of the three Canadian storages. Subject to compliance with any detailed operating plan agreed to by the entities as permitted by article XIV (2) (k) of the treaty-
-which relates to subsequent operating plans over which Canada has a veto-
-the manner of operation which will achieve the specific storage or release of storage called for in a hydroelectric operating plan consistent with optimum storage use will be at the discretion of the Canadian entity.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, the effect of the provision of the protocol is that the Canadian entity retains the right to decide how that storage will be held as a whole within Canada and retains the right to decide how it will be released in accordance with the monthly operating plan of the United States. This confers a substantial benefit and makes it possible to operate Mica creek for maximum generation at the site and at the site of the dams at Downey creek and Revelstoke when they are constructed, and gives us the opportunity to reregulate that same water when it reaches the high Arrow dam. It might be useful to point out to the house the function of the high Arrow dam in this connection. There has been a great deal of criticism by General McNaughton and by others, which has been echoed by members of the New Democratic party in this house, that a great

Columbia River Treaty deal of the storage control area is very close to the Canadian border. I should like to point out that this is for the express purpose of making certain that at the highest head in Canada, that is at Mica creek, the storage which will be held behind the dam can be operated solely and exclusively, subject to the minimal provision for flood control, for the benefit of maximum Canadian power generation. The high Arrow dam is to provide a means of reregulating the flow of the waters for the people across the border in accordance with the treaty.
But that is not what the United States engineers say.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would advise the hon. member for Kootenay West, if he is going to participate in this particularly interesting but particularly complicated discussion, that he should read the protocol and, what may be more difficult for him, try to understand its contents.
Turning again to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam as reported on page 497 of Hansard, I find he makes reference to the restriction of the Canadian right to operate these storages in view of the obligation to deliver to the United States flood control, that is control against those critical situations when there will be flooding and risk of damage downstream. I would bring to the attention of the house the fact that the problems involved in this regard have been specifically met by the terms of paragraph 1 of the protocol. As the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) pointed out this afternoon, the rather obscure terms of the treaty with regard to these provisions have been defined more closely by the protocol. There is provision for flood control by Canada only after a number of eventualities: First, only after a certain flood level of historically determined proportions has been reached. Second, only after all United States storages in the entire Columbia basin have been used for the purpose of restraining the flood. Third, by subparagraph 3 of paragraph 1 of the protocol the Canadian entity has the right of approval of the United States flood control, and in the absence of agreement there is a provision for a form of arbitration through the permanent engineering board.
Then, I should like to call attention to the statement of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam as recorded on page 497 of Hansard to the effect that the Libby dam in the United States will be controlled by the United States. He says that if it feels it would be to its disadvantage, then it does not have to vary the operation. I point out, Mr. Speaker, first that the operation of the Libby dam will be specifically subject to a long-standing order of the
[Mr. Macdonald.)
international joint commission in respect of the level of the water at Kootenay lake. This particular order restricts both Canada and the United States in altering the level of Kootenay lake, and it is of particular value to Canada in this particular instance because it restricts specifically the extent to which the United States can vary or have exceptionally high peaks in flood release.
Then, the protocol by paragraph 5 expressly stipulates that the Libby dam is to be co-ordinated in its operation for the purpose of achieving the additional maximum power generation at the west Kootenay plant of 200,000 kilowatt years per annum.
Once again, at page 497 of Hansard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam commits an error which I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West might have drawn to his attention, because it is purely an error in geography. The hon. member makes reference to a statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) in respect of diversion of the Kootenay into the Columbia and then goes on to say:
This, again, is a matter of giving a legal right which has little or no value because since the Americans are the upstream nation in the case of the Kootenay, and since they will be operating a dam at the Libby, they will have the right to determine how much water would come into Canada-
I would point out that the diversion in question is the diversion to the headwaters of the Columbia river upstream from Libby and in this particular case Canada is the upstream country, so that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) does not appear to have realized that.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam at page 498 of Hansard for Tuesday, March 3, remarks which have already been dealt with by a number of other speakers on both sides of the house, who pointed out that the hon. member had asserted that the McNaughton plan would flood less land. I would remind the house again, as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) did this afternoon, that the McNaughton plan would flood twice as much land as will the plan for development of the basin, provided for by the treaty.
We are talking about it in terms of agricultural land.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We get a lot of useful advice from the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who was passing on advice the other night to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. He apparently passed to him a copy of the "Engineering and Contract Record", from which the hon. member

read, as recorded at the bottom of page 498 of Hansard, and when questioned as to the date of that he replied:
My colleague tells me it is September, 1963.
The document in question is actually September, 1962, and perhaps this typifies better than anything else the information on which the hon. member bases his speeches.
He referred to an article by Mr. James Ripley, who made the following statement:
The present treaty places three of the four major dams (high Arrow. Libby, and Duncan) virtually on the American border where they are absolutely useless for any purpose except regulating U.S. flows.
As I have pointed out, this is quite clearly wrong. In the first place the Libby dam has a contributing effect on the west Kootenay plants by adding 200,000 kilowatt years per annum to the West Kootenay plants. Second, I would point out that the treaty and the engineering plans for Duncan lake provide for additional at-site power there. Third, I would point out that, in addition to the Libby operation, the Duncan lake operation will add additional power benefits to the west Kootenay plants.
The article by Mr. Ripley continues:
We cannot produce a kilowatt of at-site power for Canada at any of these dams.
I think, however, I have pointed out the fallacy of that.
The fourth dam (Mica) will produce some power but will always sacrifice part of its potential output because the treaty says it must be operated primarily for U.S. regulation.
I would point out that the changes made in the operating provisions with respect to the watershed will permit Canada to operate the entire storage as a whole, and permit Canada to maximize the entire operation at Mica and reregulate the water flow at the high Arrow dam.
Better read annex A.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You had better read annex A, and had better read the protocol as well.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam went on like some bright-eyed sorcerer's apprentice, bouncing from watershed to watershed, from the Fraser to the Columbia, and to the Saskatchewan, and pointing out how he was going to use the same water flow from the Columbia river for mutually exclusive purposes.
He pointed out that he was backing the McNaughton plan, but I wonder if he realizes that the plan more commonly associated with General McNaughton provides for the construction of dams at Bull river, Luxor and 20220-401
Columbia River Treaty Dorr, and also provides for the diversion of 15 million acre feet from Revelstoke canyon to the Fraser headwaters.
I would point out that the recent reports of the B.C. Engineering Company, recently tabled in the house, established the cost of the McNaughton plan as in excess of $2 billion.
That is not so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Read it again. You have a lot to learn. It also pointed out that it envisages a grave risk of destroying the Fraser fishery. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had a great deal to say about the creation of jobs in the British Columbia area. I wonder what his supporters in the lower mainland area and lower Fraser valley think of the cavalier way in which he casts away Canada's $50 million fishing industry.
You had better stay in Toronto, my boy.
You better go back to Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would be lucky if they even let him stay there, after that. At the same time the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam seems to talk about creating downstream benefits on the Columbia river, that is, to permit the flow to continue on down the Columbia river, the mainstream of the Columbia river, in lieu of the downstream benefits. He also laid great stress on diversion for irrigation purposes and power production on the prairies, particularly at the South Saskatchewan dam.
I would point out to the house that a necessary corollary for irrigation purposes is a loss in power benefits to British Columbia, in two ways. The first is because of the extra power needed to pump the water over the great divide on to the eastern slopes of the Rockies, and second because the five million acre feet or so that has been estimated for this purpose would result in a net loss of power, by reason of the lower generation at Mica creek.
Should we not sell it to our fellow Canadians before we sell it to the United States?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not if we get as much for it as this.
Don't take that off the record.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made some reference to the fact that he was critical of the observation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in saying that we would have the right to

Columbia River Treaty divert water across the Rockies tor irrigation purposes. I would just like to remind the house, and in particular the hon. member, of some of the practical facts involved in so-called diversion for irrigation on the prairies.
As he is perhaps aware, the Saskatchewan Power Corporation, over which at one time he apparently had some control-perhaps they are not telling him much now-had a study made for it by the Crippen-Wright engineering firm in March, 1962, on the possible use of eastern and western slope flows for irrigation on the prairies. These were the plans proposed by Crippen-Wright, in their order of priority: 1. That the North Saskatchewan and Clearwater rivers could be diverted to the extent of over 1,900,000 acre feet, at a cost of 40 cents per acre foot. 2. That the diversion of the Athabasca into the North Saskatchewan would provide an additional 4,500,000 acre feet at a cost of $1.60 per acre foot. 3. The diversion of the Peace river into the North Saskatchewan, which would allow 19 million acre feet at a cost per acre foot of $2.70. 4. The diversion of the upper Fraser into the Athabasca, and hence by the system previously discussed, down into the South Saskatchewan, giving 1,090,000 acre feet at a cost of $3.10 per acre foot, and the fifth alternative, in the order of priorities, and which would be ten times as expensive as the first scheme, was the proposed diversion from the Columbia river of 5,430,000 acre feet at a cost of $4.60 per acre foot.
The hon. member insisted that we talk in realities. I shall make the same reply to him. Let us talk about realities on the question of diversion flows for irrigation on the prairies.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make reference to a report by an American consulting firm, which was hired by the state of Washington, and which deals with the advantages which the Americans see as coming from this treaty.
Ten o'clock.
That will give you a chance to have more notes prepared for tomorrow morning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will give you a chance to read the protocol.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the acting house leader if he would outline the business for tomorrow, and such part of next week as he knows about?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall continue with this debate. When it is concluded we will take up the resolutions pertaining to the setting up of the committees. First we will deal with the setting up of the special committee on procedure; second, the committee relating to defence matters; third, the committee on drugs, insecticides, pesticides and other noxious substances, and fourth the committee on consumer credit. Then we will take the second reading of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions, and then the resolution relating to the appointment of an additional judge of the exchequer court, under the Judges Act.	[DOT]
It being three minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, March 6, 1964
